narrative:
The predictive model places your chance of failing the bar exam on the first attempt at 54.8%, meaning that based on the factors it examines, you are slightly more likely to fail than pass. That elevated risk is the immediate reason your law school application was denied.

The single most influential factor in this decision is your academic standing at the end of your third year. You finished in the lowest decile of your class, a position that stands in stark contrast to the accepted-student average of around the sixth decile. This is a critical signal because strong performance in later law school years is closely tied to bar exam success, and the model weighs that heavily. So even though you also finished in the lowest decile in your first year, it is your third-year rank that most damages your application.

Your LSAT score of 36, although slightly below the accepted-student average of about 37, actually works in your favor in the model, pushing toward a lower chance of failure. Likewise, your undergraduate GPA of 3.00, a bit below the 3.23 average, also contributes positively overall. These two credentials suggest you have a reasonable intellectual foundation, but they cannot offset the more powerful negative signal from your class rank.

To improve your chances, consider retaking your final year to lift your class standing, or enroll in a bar preparation program and submit a new application with evidence of improved academic performance. Addressing the root cause—your low class percentile—is the surest way to change this outcome.
